newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung to Beijing, China unveils handover party.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung to Beijing, China unveils handover party.

text.p: China unveiled on Tuesday a plan for lavish celebrations marking Hong Kong's return on July 1, and future leader Tung Chee-hwa prepared to go to Beijing to discuss the remaining handover hurdles.
Hong Kong will shed its 156-year-old British colonial masters at midnight on June 30, when it will become a quasi autonomous capitalist zone of Communist-ruled China.
The grand finale marking the historic handover of the British colony to China will last for about 45 minutes, the official Xinhua news agency said.
More than 4,000 invited guests will attend the finale in the grand hall of Hong Kong's new Convention and Exhibition Centre, starting at 11:30 p.m. (1530 GMT) on June 30.
As midnight approaches, the Union Jack and the colonial Hong Kong flag will be lowered slowly. At midnight the Chinese red flag and the new Hong Kong flag will be hoisted, Xinhua said.

As dawn breaks on Tuesday, July 1, the Chinese army will begin deployments across the border into Hong Kong in a public display of the resumption of Chinese sovereignty over the wealthy community of 6.4 million people.
At 10 a.m. (0200 GMT) on July 1 the new Hong Kong government, led by shipping magnate Tung, is to be inaugurated at the Hong Kong Coliseum on the Kowloon peninsula.
An aide of Tung's told Reuters his agenda for Beijing talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on Wednesday was not clear but they would tackle any remaining handover issues.
These include Tung's plan, foisted on him by China's parliament, to limit civil liberties such as the right to protest and to ban foreign funding of local political groups.
The plan, which Tung subjected to a public feedback exercise, has stirred outrage in pro-democracy circles and provoked strong criticism from Britain and the United States.
Tung is under pressure from critics -- who include the Law Society and Bar Association representing most Hong Kong lawyers -- to alter the plan and make it less intimidating.
In Washington, U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said there should be no separation of economic and political freedoms in Hong Kong after China takes over.

Members of the Tung government-in-waiting have said Hong Kong people care about their economic freedoms and not so much about political freedoms. The future government plans to curtail political liberties and replace the elected legislature.
"The crucial thing to recognise for Hong Kong going forward is that there are no firewalls between economic freedom and freedom in its many other dimensions," Summers warned.

Hong Kong's economic success -- it is the eighth largest trading economy in the world and has the world's highest per capita ownership of Rolls Royce cars -- could only be maintained if it enjoyed free flow of information and ideas, Summers said.
Britain's new Foreign Secretary Robin Cook called Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten on Monday and said a smooth handover to China was one of the new Labour government's top priorities.
"The government is fully committed to the well-being of Hong Kong, in particular the rule of law and the rights and freedoms enjoyed there," a foreign office spokesman in London said.
Tung called on new Prime Minister Tony Blair to make a fresh start in Sino-British ties, soured by disputes over Hong Kong, especially Patten's democratisation of the territory.

In a newspaper interview Tung urged London to "put behind us all the arguments, to sit down, to say these things have to be done and move forward continuously in the interest of the six and a half million people of Hong Kong."
